370APPENDIX II
1THE CONSTITUTION (APPLICATION TO JAMMU AND KASHMIR)
ORDER, 2019
C.O. 272
In exercise of the powers conferred by clause (1) of article 370 of the
Constitution, the President, with the concurrence of the Government of State of
Jammu and Kashmir, is pleased to make the following Order:—
1. (1) This Order may be called the Constitution (Application to Jammu
and Kashmir) Order, 2019.
(2) It shall come into force at once, and shall thereupon supersede the
Constitution (Application to Jammu and Kashmir) Order, 1954 as amended
from time to time.
2. All the provisions of the Constitution, as amended from time to time,
shall apply in relation to the State of Jammu and Kashmir and the exceptions
and modifications subject to which they shall so apply shall be as follows:–
To article 367, there shall be added the following clause, namely:
“(4) For the purposes of this Constitution as it applies in relation
to the State of Jammu and Kashmir–
(a) references to this Constitution or to the
provisions thereof shall be construed as references to the
Constitution or the provisions thereof as applied in relation
tothe said State;
(b) references to the person for the time being
recognized by the President on the recommendation of the
Legislative Assembly of the State as the Sadar-i-Riyasat of
Jammu and Kashmir, acting on the advice of the Council of
Ministers of the State for the time being in office, shall be
construed as references to the Governor of Jammu and
Kashmir;
(c) references to the Government of the said State
shall be construed as including references to the Governor
of Jammu and Kashmir acting on the advice of his Council
of Ministers; and
(d) in proviso to clause (3) of article 370 of this
Constitution, the expression “Constituent Assembly of the
State referred to in clause (2)” shall read “Legislative
Assembly of the State”.”
1.Published with the Ministry of Law and Justice, (Legislative Department) notification
No. G.S.R. 551 (E), dated the 5th August, 2019, Gazette of India, Extraordinary,
Part II, Section 3, Sub-section (i).

371APPENDIX III
1DECLRATION UNDER ARTICLE 370(3) OF THE CONSTITUTION
C.O. 273
In exercise of the powers conferred by clause (3) of article 370 read
with clause (1) of article 370 of the Constitution of India, the President, on the
recommendation of Parliament, is pleased to declare that, as from the 6th
August, 2019, all clauses of the said article 370 shall cease to be operative
except the following which shall read as under, namely:—
“370. All provisions of this Constitution, as amended from time to
time, without any modifications or exceptions, shall apply to the State of
Jammu and Kashmir notwithstanding anything contrary contained in
article 152 or article 308 or any other article of this Constitution or any
other provision of the Constitution of Jammu and Kashmir or any law,
document, judgement, ordinance, order, by-law, rule, regulation,
notification, custom or usage having the force of law in the territory of
India, or any other instrument, treaty or agreement as envisaged under
article 363 or otherwise.”.
1.Published with the Ministry of Law and Justice, (Legislative Department) notification
No. G.S.R. 562(E), dated the 6th August, 2019, Gazette of India, Extraordinary, Part II,
Section 3, Sub-section (i).

PART I: CONSTITUTION OF INDIA

Constitution - Introduction & Preamble
The Constitution is the foundational legal document of India, adopted on 26th November 1949 and effective from 26th January 1950.
It establishes the sovereignty of the people, guarantees fundamental rights, and lays down the government framework.
The Preamble outlines its core objectives: justice, liberty, equality, and fraternity, assuring dignity of the individual and unity of the nation.

Constitution - Salient Features
India's Constitution is the longest written constitution in the world.
It establishes a sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic.
Key features include: federal structure with unitary bias, parliamentary government, independence of judiciary, fundamental rights, directive principles, fundamental duties, and a system of checks and balances between the three organs of government.

Article 1 - Union and Its Territory
Article 1 declares India as a "Union of States" rather than a federation of states. The territory of India comprises: (a) territories of states, (b) union territories, and (c) territories that may be acquired. This provision emphasizes the indestructible nature of the Indian Union while allowing reorganization of states under Article 3.

Articles 2-4 - Admission and Formation of New States
Parliament may admit new states into the Union or establish new states on terms and conditions it deems fit. Article 3 empowers Parliament to form new states by separation of territory, uniting states, or altering boundaries. Such bills require Presidential recommendation and reference to concerned state legislatures, though their views are not binding.

Articles 5-11 - Citizenship
Citizenship provisions at commencement: persons domiciled in India with either birth in India, either parent born in India, or ordinary residence for 5+ years became citizens. Article 11 empowers Parliament to regulate citizenship by law. The Citizenship Act, 1955 provides for acquisition by birth, descent, registration, naturalization, and incorporation of territory.
Citizenship Act, 1955 - Acquisition Modes
Citizenship by birth: born in India on/after 26.1.1950. By descent: born outside India to Indian parent(s). By registration: persons of Indian origin, spouses of citizens, minor children. By naturalization: foreigners resident in India for 12 months preceding application and 11 years total. By incorporation of territory: persons in territories becoming part of India become citizens.
Citizenship - Loss and Termination
Citizenship can be lost by: (a) Renunciation - voluntary giving up; (b) Termination - acquiring another country's citizenship automatically terminates Indian citizenship; (c) Deprivation - compulsory termination by government for citizenship acquired by fraud, disloyalty to Constitution, unlawful trade with enemy during war, or imprisonment outside India for 2+ years.
Citizenship Amendment Act, 2019
CAA, 2019 amended the Citizenship Act to provide citizenship to persecuted minorities (Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis, Christians) from Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Pakistan who entered India by 31.12.2014. It reduced naturalization residency requirement from 11 to 5 years. The Act exempted tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Tripura from its application.

Part III - Fundamental Rights: Introduction

Fundamental Rights (Articles 12-35) are justiciable rights guaranteed against state action. They act as limitations on state power and ensure individual liberty. Available against state (Article 12 defines state) and some rights against private individuals. Article 13 declares laws inconsistent with fundamental rights void to the extent of inconsistency.

Article 12 - Definition of State
State includes: (a) Government and Parliament of India, (b) Government and Legislature of states, (c) all local authorities (municipalities, panchayats, district boards), (d) other authorities (statutory authorities, instrumentalities of state like LIC, ONGC, universities). Courts have expanded "other authorities" to include any body controlled and financially supported by government.

Article 13 - Laws Inconsistent with Fundamental Rights
All laws in force before Constitution commencement, inconsistent with fundamental rights, shall be void. The state shall not make any law taking away or abridging fundamental rights. "Law" includes ordinances, orders, bye-laws, rules, regulations, notifications, customs having force of law. Constitutional amendments are not "law" under Article 13 (Kesavananda Bharati case).
Doctrine of Eclipse
Under Article 13, pre-constitutional laws inconsistent with fundamental rights become eclipsed or dormant. They are not dead but overshadowed by fundamental rights. If the fundamental right is subsequently amended to remove inconsistency, the eclipsed law revives and becomes operative without re-enactment. This doctrine applies only to pre-constitutional laws, not post-constitutional laws.
Doctrine of Severability
Article 13 provides that if a law is inconsistent with fundamental rights, only the offending part is void, not the entire law, provided the invalid part is severable from the rest. The court examines whether after removing the unconstitutional portion, the remaining part can stand independently and reflects the legislature's intention.
Waiver of Fundamental Rights
Fundamental rights cannot be waived by individuals. They are not merely private rights but embody public policy and constitutional morality. The Supreme Court held in Basheshar Nath v. CIT that fundamental rights are transcendental and cannot be waived even by express consent, as they exist to protect citizens against state action.

Article 14 - Equality Before Law
Article 14 guarantees equality before law and equal protection of laws. "Equality before law" is negative concept meaning no privilege, no person above law. "Equal protection of laws" is positive concept meaning equal treatment in equal circumstances. It permits reasonable classification based on intelligible differentia having rational relation to objective sought.
Article 14 - Reasonable Classification Test
For classification to be valid: (1) It must be founded on intelligible differentia distinguishing persons grouped together from others left out. (2) The differentia must have rational relation to the statute's objective. Classification cannot be arbitrary; it must be based on real and substantial distinctions bearing just and reasonable relation to the object.
Article 14 - Arbitrariness Test
Since E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974), Article 14 also strikes down arbitrary state action. Equality is antithetic to arbitrariness. Wherever state action is arbitrary and unreasonable, it violates Article 14. This expanded concept means even single-person decisions can be challenged if arbitrary, without requiring classification comparison.

Article 15 - Prohibition of Discrimination
Article 15(1) prohibits discrimination against citizens on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth. Article 15(2) ensures access to shops, public restaurants, wells, tanks, roads, and public places without discrimination. This promotes social equality and prohibits exclusion based on untouchability or other discriminatory practices.
Article 15 - Special Provisions
Article 15(3) permits special provisions for women and children. Article 15(4) allows advancement of socially and educationally backward classes, SCs, STs. Article 15(5) enables their admission to educational institutions including private ones. Article 15(6) permits 10% reservation for economically weaker sections (EWS) based on income and asset criteria.

Article 16 - Equality in Public Employment
Article 16 guarantees equality of opportunity in public employment. No discrimination based on religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth, residence. It permits: (a) residence requirements for specific states, (b) reservation for backward classes not adequately represented, (c) religious requirements for religious institutions, (d) SC/ST reservation in promotions with seniority.
Article 16 - Reservation Jurisprudence
Reservation under Article 16(4) is not a fundamental right but an enabling provision. Creamy layer exclusion applies to OBCs. Total reservation cannot exceed 50% (Indra Sawhney case). Reservation in promotions requires quantifiable data of backwardness and inadequacy of representation. 103rd Amendment (2019) introduced 10% EWS reservation beyond 50% limit.

Article 17 - Abolition of Untouchability
Article 17 abolishes "untouchability" and forbids its practice in any form. Enforcement of disability arising from untouchability is a punishable offense. The Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 (formerly Untouchability Offenses Act) prescribes penalties for preventing任何人 from entering places of worship, taking water from tanks, or accessing public facilities.

Article 18 - Abolition of Titles
Article 18 abolishes titles except military and academic distinctions. No citizen shall accept any title from foreign state. No foreign title holder accepting office of profit under state requires President's consent. However, national awards like Bharat Ratna, Padma awards are not titles under Article 18 but recognitions of merit, upheld by Supreme Court.

Article 19 - Six Freedoms: Introduction
Article 19 guarantees six freedoms: (a) speech and expression, (b) assembly peacefully without arms, (c) formation of associations, (d) movement throughout India, (e) residence and settlement anywhere, (f) profession, occupation, trade, business. All freedoms subject to reasonable restrictions in interests of sovereignty, security, public order, decency, morality, etc.
Article 19(1)(a) - Freedom of Speech
Freedom of speech includes right to express opinions, publish, propagate, receive information, and communicate through any medium. It encompasses press freedom, right to know, right to remain silent, and commercial speech. Reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2) for: sovereignty, security, foreign relations, public order, defamation, contempt of court, incitement to offense.
Article 19(1)(b) - Right to Assemble
Citizens have right to assemble peacefully and without arms. This includes meetings, processions, gatherings. Restrictions under Article 19(3) for sovereignty, public order. Section 144 CrPC can regulate assemblies. Police cannot refuse permission arbitrarily. Processions cannot be banned entirely but can be regulated regarding time, place, and route to prevent disturbance.
Article 19(1)(c) - Right to Form Associations
Right includes forming unions, cooperative societies, political parties, trade unions, companies. Restrictions under Article 19(4) for sovereignty, public order, morality. While government can derecognize associations, it cannot ban their formation entirely unless satisfied about unlawful activities. Trade unions enjoy this right subject to reasonable regulations.
Article 19(1)(d) & (e) - Movement and Residence
Right to move freely throughout India and reside/settle anywhere. These rights promote national unity and economic integration. Restrictions under Articles 19(5) for interests of general public or protection of Scheduled Tribes. Tribal areas may have entry restrictions. No state can impose permanent internal travel restrictions on citizens.
Article 19(1)(g) - Right to Profession
Right to practice any profession, carry on occupation, trade, business. Includes right not to trade, right to closed shop, right to choose vocation. Restrictions under Article 19(6) for: professional qualifications, technical requirements, state monopolies, prohibition of dangerous trades, and reasonable restrictions in public interest. Monopolies must be based on valid legislation.

Article 20 - Protection in Respect of Conviction
Article 20 contains three protections: (1) Ex post facto laws - no conviction for act not offense at time of commission, but lesser punishment can apply retrospectively. (2) Double jeopardy - no person prosecuted and punished twice for same offense. (3) Self-incrimination - no compulsion to be witness against oneself.
Article 20(3) - Protection Against Self-Incrimination
No person accused of offense shall be compelled to be witness against himself. Protection extends to: (a) accused person, (b) compulsion, (c) giving evidence against self. Includes testimonial evidence, documents, statements. Does not cover: handwriting samples, fingerprints, blood samples, medical examination. Confessions to police are inadmissible under Evidence Act.

Article 21 - Protection of Life and Personal Liberty
"No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law." Post-Maneka Gandhi, "procedure" must be just, fair, reasonable. Article 21 now encompasses: right to livelihood, privacy, health, clean environment, speedy trial, legal aid, shelter, food, education, dignity, and all attributes making life meaningful.
Article 21 - Expanded Interpretation
Supreme Court has expanded Article 21 to include: right to die with dignity (but not suicide), right to die (passive euthanasia permitted), right to reputation, right to sleep, right against sexual harassment, right to education (now Article 21A), right to medical care, right to clean water, right to pollution-free environment, and right to emergency medical aid.
Article 21A - Right to Education
Inserted by 86th Amendment, 2002, Article 21A guarantees free and compulsory education to all children aged 6-14 years as state shall determine by law. The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 (RTE Act) implements this, requiring private schools to reserve 25% seats for disadvantaged groups and prohibiting corporal punishment.

Article 22 - Protection Against Arrest and Detention
Article 22 provides safeguards for arrested persons: (a) right to know grounds of arrest, (b) right to consult and be defended by lawyer, (c) right to be produced before magistrate within 24 hours, (d) detention beyond 24 hours only with magistrate's authority. These protections apply to punitive detention but not preventive detention.
Article 22 - Preventive Detention Provisions
Preventive detention (detention without trial) permitted under Articles 22(3)-(7). Maximum detention 3 months unless Advisory Board finds sufficient cause. Detainee entitled to grounds of detention but can be denied facts prejudicial to public interest. Parliament can prescribe maximum detention period. State laws require President's assent.

Articles 23-24 - Right Against Exploitation
Article 23 prohibits traffic in human beings, begar (forced labor without payment), and similar forms of forced labor. Violation punishable by law. Exceptions: state may impose compulsory service for public purposes without discrimination. Article 24 prohibits employment of children below 14 years in factories, mines, hazardous occupations.
Article 23 - Bonded Labour Abolition
Article 23 formed basis for Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976. Any agreement requiring rendering of service as security for debt or advance is void. All bonded labourers stand freed from any obligation to repay debt. Supreme Court has directed identification, release, and rehabilitation of bonded labourers as constitutional obligation.

Articles 25-28 - Right to Freedom of Religion
Articles 25-28 guarantee secular character: (25) freedom of conscience and free profession, practice, propagation of religion; (26) freedom to manage religious affairs; (27) freedom from taxation for promoting any religion; (28) freedom from religious instruction in state-funded educational institutions. These ensure India's equal respect for all faiths.
Article 25 - Individual Religious Freedom
Subject to public order, morality, health, all persons equally entitled to freedom of conscience and right to profess, practice, propagate religion. State can regulate secular activities associated with religious practice. State can provide for social welfare and reform or throwing open Hindu religious institutions to all classes. Essential religious practices are protected.

Article 26 - Religious Denominations
Every religious denomination has right to: (a) establish and maintain religious institutions, (b) manage its own religious affairs, (c) own and acquire property, (d) administer property according to law. "Denomination" means religious sect having common faith, organization, and designation. Administration must be in manner ordained by religious tenets, subject to state regulation.

Articles 27-28 - Religion and Taxation/Education
Article 27: No person compelled to pay taxes for promoting any particular religion. Article 28: No religious instruction in state-funded institutions. Institutions administered by religious endowments may impart religious instruction. Attendance at religious worship in recognized/aided institutions requires consent of guardian or (if adult) individual.

Articles 29-30 - Cultural and Educational Rights
Article 29: Protection of language, script, culture of minorities; no denial of admission to state-funded institutions based on religion, race, caste, language. Article 30: Minorities have right to establish and administer educational institutions; state cannot discriminate in granting aid. These protect minority identity and educational autonomy.

Article 30 - Minority Educational Institutions
Minority institutions have fundamental right to administer, including: selecting teachers, admitting students (subject to merit), charging fees, settling disputes, taking disciplinary action. Reasonable regulations permissible for excellence but not impairing minority character. Linguistic minorities also covered. Institution retains minority character even if non-minority students admitted.

Articles 31A-31D - Saving of Certain Laws
Article 31A saves land reform laws from fundamental rights challenge. Article 31B protects Acts in Ninth Schedule from judicial review on fundamental rights grounds, though subject to basic structure doctrine. Article 31C protects laws giving effect to Directive Principles. Article 31D (repealed) dealt with anti-national activities.

Article 32 - Right to Constitutional Remedies
Dr. Ambedkar called Article 32 the "heart and soul" of Constitution. It guarantees right to move Supreme Court for fundamental rights enforcement. Supreme Court has power to issue writs: habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, quo warranto, certiorari. This right cannot be suspended except as Constitution provides. It is itself a fundamental right.
Writ of Habeas Corpus
Habeas Corpus means "produce the body." It orders production of illegally detained person before court to secure release. Available against public and private detention. Application can be made by detainee or any person on their behalf. Court examines legality of detention; if illegal, orders release. Cannot be issued where detention lawful.
Writ of Mandamus
Mandamus means "we command." It commands public official, corporation, inferior court to perform public duty. Conditions: applicant must have legal right, duty must be mandatory and public, demand made and refused, no alternative remedy. Cannot issue against President, Governors, or private individuals unless they perform public functions.
Writ of Prohibition
Prohibition is issued by higher court to lower court or tribunal to prevent exceeding jurisdiction or acting contrary to law. It operates during pending proceedings, before judgment. It prevents judicial or quasi-judicial bodies from usurping jurisdiction. Grounds: lack/excess of jurisdiction, violation of natural justice, error of law apparent on face.
Writ of Certiorari
Certiorari quashes orders of inferior courts, tribunals, quasi-judicial authorities. Conditions: body must have legal authority with duty to act judicially, must have passed order exceeding jurisdiction or with error of law. Unlike prohibition (which prevents), certiorari corrects after decision. Available against administrative bodies acting judicially.
Writ of Quo Warranto
Quo Warranto means "by what authority." It inquires into legality of claim to public office. Applicant questions usurper's right to hold office. Conditions: office must be public and substantive, created by statute, person not legally qualified. Court examines appointment validity; if invalid, declares office vacant. Cannot question procedural irregularities.

Article 33 - Armed Forces and Fundamental Rights
Parliament may restrict or abrogate fundamental rights for members of Armed Forces, paramilitary forces, police, intelligence agencies to ensure proper discharge of duties and discipline. Restrictions must relate to forces' requirements. Air Force Act, Army Act, Navy Act contain such restrictions. Parliament's power is exclusive and plenary in this regard.

Article 34 - Martial Law
When martial law declared in any area, Parliament may indemnify persons acting in maintenance or restoration of order and validate acts done under martial law. Indemnity can extend to acts otherwise illegal. Article 34 does not authorize martial law imposition; it only deals with consequences after Parliament validates acts during martial law.

Article 35 - Legislation on Fundamental Rights
Parliament has exclusive power to make laws on: (a) prescribing residence requirements for public employment (Article 16), (b) specifying offenses under Article 17 (untouchability), (c) prescribing punishment for acts declared offenses under Part III, (d) providing for martial law indemnity (Article 34), (e) presidential orders for certain classes (Articles 31A, 31B).

Part IV - Directive Principles: Introduction
Directive Principles of State Policy (Articles 36-51) are non-justiciable guidelines for government to establish social and economic democracy. They aim at welfare state, social justice, and economic equality. Though not enforceable by courts, they are fundamental in governance and duty of state to apply in making laws. They complement fundamental rights.

Article 36-37 - Nature of Directive Principles
Article 36 defines state same as Article 12. Article 37 declares DPSP not enforceable by courts but principles fundamental in governance; state shall apply them in law-making. This creates constitutional obligation; governments ignoring them risk political accountability. Courts can use DPSP to interpret fundamental rights and test constitutional validity.

Article 38 - Social Order
State shall secure social order promoting welfare of people. It shall minimize inequalities in income, status, facilities, opportunities not only among individuals but also groups residing in different areas or engaged in different vocations. This principle guides policies for economic justice and reducing concentration of wealth.

Article 39 - Certain Principles of Policy
State shall direct policy securing: (a) adequate livelihood for all citizens, (b) community ownership of material resources for common good, (c) prevention of wealth concentration against public interest, (d) equal pay for equal work for men and women, (e) protection of children and youth from exploitation, (f) free and compulsory education (now Article 21A).
Article 39A - Equal Justice and Free Legal Aid
Inserted by 42nd Amendment, Article 39A requires state to ensure equal justice and provide free legal aid to economically disadvantaged. It mandates ensuring opportunities for securing justice not denied by economic or other disabilities. This principle supports Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 establishing legal aid machinery.

Articles 40-43 - Village Panchayats to Living Wage
Article 40: Organize village panchayats with powers of self-government. Article 41: Right to work, education, public assistance in unemployment, old age, sickness, disability. Article 42: Just and humane conditions of work, maternity relief. Article 43: Living wage for workers, decent standard of life, social and cultural opportunities.

Article 43A - Workers' Participation
Inserted by 42nd Amendment, Article 43A requires state to secure workers' participation in management of industries. Various industries have implemented schemes through statutes like Industrial Disputes Act, Companies Act providing for worker directors. The principle aims at industrial democracy and harmonious industrial relations.

Articles 44-48 - Uniform Civil Code to Agriculture
Article 44: State shall endeavor to secure Uniform Civil Code for all citizens. Article 45: Provision for early childhood care and education for children below 6 years. Article 46: Promote educational and economic interests of SCs, STs, weaker sections. Article 47: Raise nutrition levels, improve public health. Article 48: Organize scientific agriculture, animal husbandry.

Articles 48A-51 - Environment to International Peace
Article 48A (42nd Amendment): Protect and improve environment, safeguard forests and wildlife. Article 49: Protect monuments, places of national importance. Article 50: Separate judiciary from executive in public services. Article 51: Promote international peace and security, maintain just and honorable relations, foster respect for international law.

DPSP - Implementation and Conflict Resolution
DPSP implemented through various laws: Minimum Wages Act, Land Reforms, Panchayati Raj, Maternity Benefit, Equal Remuneration, Environment Protection. Where fundamental rights and DPSP conflict, courts attempt harmonious construction (Minerva Mills). Neither absolute over other; both together form core of constitutional philosophy.

Part IVA - Fundamental Duties: Article 51A
Inserted by 42nd Amendment (1976), Fundamental Duties remind citizens of their obligations. Originally 10 duties, 86th Amendment (2002) added duty of parent/guardian to provide education to child aged 6-14. Duties non-justiciable but courts consider them when interpreting laws and can be promoted through education and awareness.

Article 51A - List of Fundamental Duties
It shall be duty of every citizen: (a) respect Constitution, national flag, anthem; (b) cherish noble ideals of freedom struggle; (c) uphold sovereignty, unity, integrity; (d) defend country; (e) promote common brotherhood, dignity of women; (f) preserve rich heritage; (g) protect environment; (h) develop scientific temper; (i) safeguard public property; (j) strive for excellence; (k) provide education opportunities to child.

Part V - Union Executive: President

Article 52: President of India. Article 53: Executive power vested in President, exercised directly or through subordinate officers. Supreme commander of armed forces. Elected by Electoral College comprising elected MPs and MLAs through proportional representation with single transferable vote. Term: 5 years. Qualifications: citizen, 35 years, eligible for Lok Sabha.

Article 72 - President's Pardoning Power
President has power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites, remissions of punishment, or suspend, remit, commute sentences in: (a) cases punishable by court-martial, (b) offenses against Union law, (c) death sentences. This is executive power exercised on aid and advice of Council of Ministers, subject to judicial review for arbitrariness.

Articles 74-75 - Council of Ministers
Article 74: There shall be Council of Ministers with Prime Minister at head to aid and advise President. 42nd Amendment made advice binding, but 44th Amendment enabled President to require reconsideration. Article 75: PM appointed by President, other ministers on PM's advice. Ministers hold office during President's pleasure, collectively responsible to Lok Sabha.

Article 76 - Attorney General of India
President appoints Attorney General, must be person qualified to be Supreme Court judge. Holds office during President's pleasure, receives remuneration President determines. Duties: advise Government on legal matters, perform other legal duties assigned, discharge functions conferred by Constitution. Right of audience in all courts. Can participate in Parliament without vote.

Articles 79-81 - Parliament: Composition
Parliament consists of President, Lok Sabha (House of People), Rajya Sabha (Council of States). Lok Sabha maximum 552 members: 530 from states, 20 from UTs, 2 Anglo-Indians nominated (37th Amendment Act, 2020 removed nomination). Rajya Sabha maximum 250: 238 elected by states/UTs, 12 nominated by President for expertise in literature, science, art, social service.

Parliamentary Privileges: Articles 105, 194
Freedom of speech in Parliament (Article 105). No liability for anything said or vote in Parliament or committees; no proceedings in court for publication of reports, papers, votes, proceedings by authority of House. Courts have no jurisdiction over proceedings irregularities. Privileges include right to exclude strangers, prohibit publication, punish contempt.

Articles 107-122 - Legislative Procedure
Bills may originate in either House except Money Bills (only Lok Sabha). After passage by both Houses, presented to President for assent. President can give assent, withhold assent, or return (except Money Bills) for reconsideration. On reconsideration, if passed again, President must assent. Financial matters governed by Articles 112-117.

Article 123 - Ordinance Making Power
When Parliament not in session and circumstances require immediate action, President may promulgate ordinances having same force as Acts. Must be laid before Parliament when it reassembles; ceases to operate after 6 weeks unless disapproved earlier. Cannot be used for matters requiring constitutional amendment or if both Houses in session.

Articles 124-147 - Supreme Court: Composition
Supreme Court consists of Chief Justice and 33 other judges (total 34). Appointed by President after consultation with CJI and other judges. Qualifications: citizen, 5 years as High Court judge or 10 years as advocate or distinguished jurist. Retire at 65. Can resign by writing to President. Removal by impeachment for proved misbehavior or incapacity.

Supreme Court - Jurisdiction
Original jurisdiction: disputes between Centre-states, enforcement of fundamental rights. Appellate jurisdiction: constitutional, civil, criminal appeals from High Courts. Advisory jurisdiction (Article 143): President may refer questions of law or public importance. Review powers: can review its judgments. Curative petition: last resort to prevent miscarriage of justice.

Article 136 - Special Leave Petition
Supreme Court may grant special leave to appeal from any judgment, decree, determination, sentence of any court or tribunal in India except military tribunals. This is discretionary power not appealable. Wide in scope but exercised sparingly when substantial question of law involved or grave injustice shown. Cannot review factual findings unless perverse.

Articles 148-151 - Comptroller and Auditor General
CAG appointed by President, holds office for 6 years or until age 65. Audits accounts of Union, states, government companies, authorities. Reports to President/Governor for laying before Parliament/legislature. Independent of executive; cannot be appointed to further government office after retirement. Ensures financial accountability and transparency.

Part VI - State Executive: Governor
Articles 153-162: Governor appointed by President, holds office during pleasure. Qualifications: citizen, 35 years, not Member of Parliament/legislature. Executive power of state vested. Appoints Chief Minister, other ministers on CM's advice. Discretionary powers: reserving bills for President, recommending President's rule, administering scheduled areas.

Article 163 - Council of Ministers in State
Council of Ministers with Chief Minister at head to aid and advise Governor except where Governor required to act in discretion. Ministers appointed by Governor on CM's advice, hold office during Governor's pleasure, collectively responsible to Legislative Assembly. Governor's satisfaction in discretionary matters not subject to court review.

Article 165 - Advocate General of State
Governor appoints person qualified to be High Court judge as Advocate General. Holds office during Governor's pleasure, receives remuneration Governor determines. Duty to advise state government on legal matters and perform legal duties assigned. Right of audience in all courts within state and can participate in legislature without vote.

Articles 168-212 - State Legislature
States may have Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha) and in some states Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad). Legislative Assembly members elected directly; maximum 500, minimum 60. Legislative Council members (1/3 of Assembly, min 40) elected by various constituencies. Legislative procedure similar to Parliament. Money Bills originate only in Assembly.

Articles 214-237 - State Judiciary
High Court for each state; common High Court for two or more states. Judges appointed by President after consultation with CJI, Governor, Chief Justice of High Court. Qualifications: citizen, 10 years judicial experience or 10 years advocate. Retire at 62. Superintendence over all courts in state. Writs jurisdiction under Article 226.

Article 226 - High Court's Writ Jurisdiction
Every High Court has power throughout territory to issue writs to any person, authority, government for enforcement of fundamental rights or for any other purpose. Wider than Supreme Court's Article 32 as extends to non-fundamental rights. Discretionary remedy; alternative remedy may bar but not absolute. Territorial jurisdiction based on cause of action or residence.

Articles 239-241 - Union Territories
President administers Union Territories through Administrator. Parliament can create local legislatures or Council of Ministers for UTs. High Court for UTs: some have own High Courts, others under neighboring High Courts. Legislative Assemblies in Delhi, Puducherry, Jammu & Kashmir have power to make laws on subjects in State List except those Parliament reserves.

Part IX - Panchayats: Articles 243-243O
Inserted by 73rd Amendment, 1992. Three-tier system: Gram Panchayat (village level), Panchayat Samiti (block level), Zila Parishad (district level). Direct elections to all seats; reservation for SCs/STs in proportion to population; 1/3 seats reserved for women. Gram Sabha consists of village electorate. Panchayats have power to prepare plans for economic development.

Part IXA - Municipalities: Articles 243P-243ZG
Inserted by 74th Amendment, 1992. Three types: Nagar Panchayat (transitional area), Municipal Council (smaller urban), Municipal Corporation (larger urban). Wards committees in population exceeding 3 lakh. Reservation similar to panchayats. District Planning Committee and Metropolitan Planning Committee consolidate plans. State Election Commission for municipal elections.

Part IXB - Co-operative Societies: Articles 243ZH-243ZT
Inserted by 97th Amendment, 2011. Right to form co-operative societies as fundamental right (Article 19). State to provide for incorporation, regulation, winding up. Members have right to vote (one member one vote). Professional board of directors limited term. State can appoint cooperative ombudsman. Audit mandatory; defaults attract penalties.

Part XI - Centre-State Relations
Articles 245-255: Distribution of legislative powers. Union List (97 subjects): defense, foreign affairs, currency. State List (66 subjects): police, agriculture, local government. Concurrent List (47 subjects): criminal law, education, forests. Residuary powers with Parliament. Parliamentary law prevails over state law on concurrent subjects.

Articles 256-263 - Administrative Relations
States must exercise executive power to ensure compliance with Union laws. Union can give directions to states. President can entrust functions to states. Inter-State Council under Article 263 for coordinating between states. All-India Services (IAS, IPS, IFoS) serve both Union and states. Full faith and credit given to public acts of states.

Articles 264-291 - Financial Relations
Distribution of taxes: Union collects certain taxes (corporation tax, customs), states collect others (land revenue, excise on alcohol). Certain taxes shared: Union Duties of Excise, Corporation Tax. Grants-in-aid from Union to states. Finance Commission (Article 280) recommends distribution of taxes between Union and states every 5 years.

Articles 292-293 - Borrowing
Union government may borrow within India or abroad on security of Consolidated Fund of India within limits fixed by Parliament. States may borrow within India on security of Consolidated Fund of state within limits fixed by legislature. If state owes money to Union, cannot borrow without Union consent. Union can give loans to states.

Articles 294-300 - Property and Contracts
Union and states can acquire, hold, dispose of property. Succession to property, assets, rights, liabilities on partition. Suits by or against government: President or Governor sued not personally but government. Government contracts: expressed in name of President/Governor, executed by persons authorized. Personal liability of executing officers exempted.

Articles 301-307 - Trade and Commerce
Article 301: Trade, commerce, intercourse throughout India free. Parliament can impose reasonable restrictions in public interest (Article 302). States can impose reasonable restrictions on goods originating from other states if similarly applicable to intra-state (Article 303). Articles 304-307 provide exceptions and authorities for implementing these provisions.

Articles 308-323 - Services and Public Service Commissions
Recruitment and conditions of service for Union and states regulated by Parliament/legislature. Public Service Commissions (UPSC, State PSCs) constituted for recruitment. Members appointed by President/Governor, hold office for 6 years or until 62 (UPSC) or 62 (State PSC). Independent; expenses charged on Consolidated Fund. Advice government on service matters.

Articles 323A-323B - Tribunals
Parliament may provide for administrative tribunals for service matters (Article 323A). Parliament and legislatures may provide for tribunals for other matters like taxation, industrial, land reforms, election disputes (Article 323B). Tribunal decisions subject to Supreme Court's jurisdiction under Article 136 and High Courts under Articles 226/227.

Articles 324-329 - Elections
Superintendence of elections vested in Election Commission (Article 324). Commission consists of Chief Election Commissioner and such other Election Commissioners President may fix. Independence: CEC removal like Supreme Court judge. Conducts elections to Parliament, state legislatures, President, Vice-President. Delimitation of constituencies, electoral rolls preparation.

Articles 330-342 - Special Provisions for Certain Classes
Reservation of seats for SCs/STs in Lok Sabha and state Assemblies in proportion to population. Anglo-Indians may be nominated if not adequately represented (37th Amendment Act, 2020 ended this). Claims of SCs/STs to services considered. National Commission for SCs, STs, Backward Classes (Articles 338-342). President specifies backward classes.

Articles 343-351 - Official Language
Hindi in Devanagari script official language of Union; English to continue for 15 years (Article 343). Parliament may provide for continued use of English beyond 15 years (Official Languages Act, 1963). Regional languages recognized. Supreme Court and High Court proceedings in English. States adopt their official languages. Special directives for linguistic minorities.

Articles 352-360 - Emergency Provisions
Three types: National Emergency (Article 352) on war, external aggression, armed rebellion; State Emergency/President's Rule (Article 356) on failure of constitutional machinery; Financial Emergency (Article 360) on financial stability threat. During national emergency, fundamental rights under Article 19 suspended, Centre gains control over states.

Articles 361-367 - Miscellaneous Provisions
President, Governors immune from criminal proceedings during term; civil proceedings with notice. No court inquiry into their actions. Succession to Indian States rulers' privy purses abolished (26th Amendment). Interpretation provisions, definitions. Power to remove difficulties.

Article 368 - Amendment of Constitution
Parliament may amend Constitution by passing bill in each House with special majority (2/3 members present and voting, absolute majority). Certain amendments require ratification by half the states. Basic structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati) limits amending power: Parliament cannot destroy basic features like secularism, democracy, federalism, judicial review.

Major Constitutional Amendments - 1st to 24th
1st Amendment (1951): Added Ninth Schedule, saved land reforms. 7th Amendment (1956): Reorganization of states. 24th Amendment (1971): Affirmed Parliament's power to amend fundamental rights. 25th Amendment (1971): Article 31C protecting DPSP laws from fundamental rights challenge.

Major Constitutional Amendments - 42nd to 44th
42nd Amendment (1976): Added Fundamental Duties, made DPSP override fundamental rights, curtailed judicial review. 44th Amendment (1978): Restored judicial review, removed right to property from fundamental rights (made Article 300A), modified emergency provisions, protected media freedom.

Major Constitutional Amendments - 52nd to 101st
52nd Amendment (1985): Anti-defection law (Tenth Schedule). 73rd & 74th (1992): Panchayats and Municipalities. 86th (2002): Right to Education (Article 21A). 97th (2011): Co-operative societies. 101st (2016): Goods and Services Tax (GST). 103rd (2019): EWS reservation. 105th (2021): Restored states' power to identify OBCs.

PART II: BHARATIYA NYAYA SANHITA (BNS) 2023 - COMPLETE COVERAGE

BNS 2023 - Introduction and Overview
The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023 received President's assent on 25th December 2023, replacing the Indian Penal Code, 1860 after 163 years. It aims to decolonize Indian criminal law, streamline provisions relating to offences and penalties, prioritize offences against women and children, and introduce community service as punishment for petty offences .

BNS - Key Structural Changes
BNS consolidates and reorganizes criminal provisions. Number of sections reduced from 511 to 358. Offences against women and children placed first, followed by offences against state. Community service introduced as new punishment category. Definitions clarified and updated. Fines increased substantially. Gender-neutral provisions expanded .

BNS Chapter I - Preliminary
Sections 1-3: Short title, extent, commencement. Extends to whole India. Commencement date to be notified. Definitions of common terms: "act", "child", "counterfeit", "court", "death", "dishonestly", "document", "fraudulently", "gender", "good faith", "government", "injury", "illegal", "judge", "justice", "month", "movable property", "number", "oath", "offence", "person", "public servant", "reason to believe", "valuable security", "vessel", "will", "wrongful gain", "wrongful loss".

BNS Chapter II - Punishments
Section 4: Punishments: Death, imprisonment for life (meaning imprisonment for remainder of natural life), imprisonment rigorous (hard labor) or simple, forfeiture of property, fine, community service. Section 5: Commutation of sentence. Section 6: Sentences in cases of conviction of several offences. Sections 7-10: Fractions of terms of punishment .

BNS Sections 11-13 - Solitary Confinement, Limit, Enhanced Punishment
Section 11: Solitary confinement cannot exceed 3 months total in any sentence of rigorous imprisonment. Maximum 14 days at a time with intervals. Section 12: Limit of punishment for offence made up of several offences. Section 13: When act is offence by reason of injury caused, punishment enhanced by extent of injury.

BNS Sections 14-17 - Sentencing Provisions
Section 14: If act charged as offence but falls within definition of another offence, may be punished for that other. Section 15: When offence proved includes minor offence, may be convicted for minor. Section 16: Person once convicted not liable for same offence again (double jeopardy). Section 17: Punishment where fine and imprisonment specified.

BNS Section 18 - Community Service
Community service introduced as punishment for petty offences. Offender required to perform unpaid work in community as court directs. Applicable for: theft under Section 303(2) where value less than ₹5,000, receiving stolen property under Section 304(2), cheating under Section 318(2), and certain other minor offences. Implementation through probation officers .

BNS Sections 19-22 - General Exceptions: Mistake and Judicial Acts
Section 19: Act of person bound by law or justified by mistake of fact in good faith, not offence. Section 20: Act of judge when acting judicially, not offence. Section 21: Act pursuant to judgment or order of court, not offence though court may lack jurisdiction, provided acted in good faith believing court had jurisdiction .

BNS Sections 23-25 - Accident, Necessity, Child
Section 23: Accident without criminal intention or knowledge, not offence. Section 24: Act likely to cause harm but without criminal intent to cause harm, and in good faith to prevent other harm, not offence (doctrine of necessity). Section 25: Act of child under 7 years, not offence. Section 26: Act of child above 7 but under 12 years with immature understanding, not offence .

BNS Sections 27-29 - Unsound Mind, Intoxication, Consent
Section 27: Act of person of unsound mind incapable of knowing nature of act, not offence. Section 28: Act of person with mental incapacity due to intoxication without knowledge or against will, not offence if administered without knowledge or against will. Section 29: Act not offence by reason of consent, death or grievous hurt exceptions.

BNS Sections 30-33 - Consent and Minors
Section 30: Consent not free (caused by fear, misconception, unsound mind, intoxication, child under 12 years incapable of judgment), not valid consent. Section 31: Act not intended and not known to cause death or grievous hurt, with consent, not offence. Section 32: Act done in good faith for benefit of child or unsound person with consent of guardian.

BNS Sections 34-36 - Communication, Duress, Trifling Acts
Section 34: Communication made in good faith for benefit of person, not offence. Section 35: Act compelled by threats causing reasonable apprehension of instant death, not offence (except murder and offences against state punishable with death). Section 36: Act causing slight harm, not offence.

BNS Sections 37-40 - Right of Private Defense
Section 37: Nothing offence done in exercise of right of private defense. Section 38: Right extends to causing death when reasonable apprehension of death, grievous hurt, assault with intent to commit rape, unnatural lust, kidnapping, abduction, wrongful confinement, robbery, dacoity, housebreaking by night, mischief by fire on building, theft, or causing hurt.

BNS Sections 41-44 - Right of Private Defense: Extent
Section 41: Right commences when reasonable apprehension of danger arises, continues as long as continues. Section 42: Right against act of person of unsound mind etc. same as against sane. Section 43: No right against public servant acting in good faith under color of office. Section 44: No right where time to have recourse to public authorities.

BNS Sections 45-48 - Abetment
Section 45: Abetment by instigation, conspiracy, intentional aid. Section 46: Abettor. Section 47: Punishment for abetment where act abetted committed. Section 48: Same where act abetted not committed. Section 49: Abetment of act punishable with death or imprisonment for life - if act not done, imprisonment up to 7 years and fine.

BNS Sections 50-56 - Criminal Conspiracy
Section 50: Criminal conspiracy defined: agreement to do illegal act or legal act by illegal means. Section 51: Punishment: imprisonment up to 6 months or fine or both (unless other provision). Section 52: Abetment outside India of offence in India. Section 53: Punishment for criminal conspiracy to commit offence punishable with death, life imprisonment, rigorous imprisonment for 2+ years .

BNS Sections 57-61 - Offences Against State
Section 57: Waging war against India: death or life imprisonment, fine. Section 58: Conspiracy to wage war. Section 59: Collecting arms to wage war. Section 60: Concealing design to wage war. Section 61: Assault on President, Governor: imprisonment up to 7 years. Section 62: Sedition (replaced): acts endangering sovereignty, unity, integrity .

BNS Sections 63-65 - Offences Against State: Waging War
Section 63: Waging war against any Asiatic power in alliance with India. Section 64: Offences against state committed outside India. Section 65: Sedition defined: words, signs, electronic communication exciting secession, armed rebellion, separatist activities, or endangering sovereignty. Punishment: life imprisonment or up to 3 years with fine.

BNS Sections 66-73 - Offences Against Army, Navy, Air Force
Section 66: Abetting mutiny. Section 67: Abetment of mutiny actually committed. Section 68: Assaulting superior officer. Section 69: Obstructing sentry. Section 70: Person subject to certain Acts. Section 71: Unlawfully wearing soldier's garb. Section 72: False evidence to screen offender. Section 73: Harboring offender.

6. Definitions in the Code to be understood subject to exceptions .—Throughout this Code every
definition of an offence, every penal provision, and every illustration of every such definition or penal
provision, shall be understood subject to the exceptions contained in the Chapter entit led “General
Exceptions ”, though those exceptions are not repeated in such definition, penal provision, or illustration .
(a) The sections, in this Code, which contain definitions of offences, do not express that a child under seven years of age
cannot commit such offences; but the definitions are to be u nderstood subject to the general exception which provides that
nothing shall be an offence which is done by a child under seven years of age.
(b) A, a police-officer, without warrant, apprehends Z , who has committed murder. Here A is not guilty of the offence of
wrongful confinement; for he was bound by law to apprehend Z, and therefore the case falls within the general exception which
provides that “nothing is an offence which is done by a person who is bound by law to do it ”.
7. Sense of expression once explained .—Every expression which is explained in any part of this
Code, is used in every part of this Code in conformity with the explanation.

22. “Movable property ”.—The words “movable property ” are intended to include corporeal property of every
description, except land and things attached to the earth or permanently fastened to anything which is attached to the
earth.
23. “Wrongful gain ”.—“Wrongful gain ” is gain by unlawful means of property to which the person gain ing is
not legally entitled.
“Wrongful loss ”.—“Wrongful loss ” is the loss by unlawful means of property to which the person losing it is
legally entitled.
Gaining wrongfully/Losing wrongfully. —A person is said to gain wrongfully when such person retains
wrongfully, as well as when such person acquires wrongfully. A pers on is said to lose wrongfully when such person
is wrongfully kept out of any property, as well as when such person is wrongfully deprived of property.
24. “Dishonestly ”.—Whoever does anything with the intention of causing wrongful gain to one person or
wrongful loss to another person, is said to do that thing “dishonestly ”.
25. “Fraudulently ”.—A person is said to do a thing fraudulently if he does that thing with intent to defraud but
not otherwise.
26. “Reason to believe ”.—A person is said to have “reason to believe ” a thing if he has sufficient cause to
believe that thing but not otherwise.
27. “Property in possession of wife, clerk or servant ”.—When property is in the possession of a person's
wife, clerk or servant, on account of that person, it is in that person's pos session within the meaning of this Code.
Explanation .—A person employed temporarily or on a particular occasion in th e capacity of a clerk, or servant,
is a clerk or servant within the meaning of this sectio n.
28. “Counterfeit ”.—A person is said to “counterfeit ” who causes one thing to resemble another thing,
intending by means of that resemblance to practise deception, or k nowing it to be likely that deception will thereby
be practised.
1[Explanation 1.—It is not essential to counterfeiting that the imitation should be exact.
Explanation 2.—When a person causes one thing to resemble another thing, and the rese mblance is such that a
person might be deceived thereby, it shall be presumed, until the contrary is proved, that the person so causing the
one thing to resemble the other thing intended by means of that resemblan ce to practise deception or knew it to be
likely that deception would thereby be practised.]
29. “Document ”.—The word “document ” denotes any matter expressed or described upon any substance by
means of letters, figures or marks, or by more than one of those means, intended to be used, or which may be used,
as evidence of that matter.
Explanation 1 .—It is immaterial by what means or upon what substance the letters, figures or marks are formed,
or whether the evidence is intended for, or may be used in, a Cou rt of Justice, or not.
A writing expressing the terms of a contract, which may be used as eviden ce of the contract, is a document.
A cheque upon a banker is a document.
A power- of-attorney is a document.
A map or plan which is intended to be used or which may be used a s evidence, is a document.
A writing containing directions or instructions is a document.
Explanation 2 .—Whatever is expressed by means of letters, figures or marks as explained by mercantile or other usage,
shall be deemed to be expressed by such letters, figures or marks with in the meaning of this section, although the same may not
be actually expressed .
A writes his name on the back of a bill of exchange payable to his order. The meaning of the endorsement, as explained by
mercantile usage, is that the bill is to be paid to the holder. The endorsement is a document, and must be construe d in the same
manner as if the words “pay to the holder ” or words to that effect had been written over the signature.
2[29A. “Electronic record ”.—The words “electronic record ” shall have the meaning assigned to them in
clause ( t) of sub-section ( 1) of section 2 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (21 of 2 000).]

30. “Valuable security ”.—The words “valuable security ” denote a document which is, or purports to
be, a document whereby any legal right is created, extended, transferred, restricted, extingui shed or
released, or whereby any person acknowledges that he lies under legal liability, or has not a certain legal
right.
A writes his name on the back of a bill of exchange. As the effec t of this endorsement is to transfer the right to the bill to any
person who may become the unlawful holder of it, the endorsement is a “valuable security ”.
31. “A will ”.—The words “a will ” denote any testamentary document.
32. Words referring to acts include illegal omissions .—In every part of this Code, except where a
contrary intention appears from the context, words which refer to acts done ex tend also to illegal
omissions.
33. “Act”. “Omission ”.—The word “act” denotes as well as series of acts as a single act: the word
“omission ” denotes as well a series of omissions as a single omission.
1[34. Acts done by several persons in furtherance of common intention .—When a criminal act is
done by several persons in furtherance of the common intention of all, each of such persons i s liable for
that act in the same manner as if it were done by him alone.]
35. When such an act is criminal by reason of its being done with a cr iminal knowledge or
intention. —Whenever an act, which is criminal only by reason of its being done with a cri minal
knowledge or intention, is done by several persons, each of such persons who joins in the act wi th such
knowledge or intention is liable for the act in the same manner as if the act w ere done by him alone with
that knowledge or intention.
36. Effect caused partly by act and partly by omission .—Wherever the causing of a certain effect,
or an attempt to cause that effect, by an act or by an omission, is an offence, it is t o be understood that the
causing of that effect partly by an act and partly by an omission is the same offence.
A intentionally causes Z's death, partly by illegally omitting to give Z food, and party by beating Z. A has committed
murder.
37. Co-operation by doing one of several acts constituting an offence .—When an offence is
committed by means of several acts, whoever intentionally co-operates in the com mission of that offence
by doing any one of those acts, either singly or jointly with any other person, commits that offence.
(a) A and B agree to murder Z by severally and at different times g iving him small doses of poison. A and B administer the
poison according to the agreement with intent to murder Z. Z dies from th e effects the several doses of poison so administered to
him. Here A and B intentionally co-operate in the commission of murd er and as each of them does an act by which the death is
caused, they are both guilty of the offence though their acts are separate.
(b) A and B are joint jailors, and as such have the charge of Z, a prisoner, alternatively for six hours at a time. A and B,
intending to cause Z's death, knowingly co-operate in causing that e ffect by illegally omitting, each during the time of his
attendance, to furnish Z with food supplied to them for that purpo se. Z dies of hunger. Both A and B, are guilty of the murder of
Z.
(c) A, a jailor, has the charge of Z, a prisoner. A, intending to cause Z' s death, illegally omits to supply Z with food; in
consequence of which Z is much reduced in strength, but the starv ation is not sufficient to cause his death. A is dismissed from
his office, and B succeeds him. B, without collusion or co-operati on with A, illegally omits to supply Z with food, knowing that
he is likely thereby to cause Z's death. Z dies of hunger. B is guil ty of murder, but, as A did not co-operate with B. A is guilty
only of an attempt to commit murder.
38. Persons concerned in criminal act may be guilty of different offences .—Where several
persons are engaged or concerned in the commission of a criminal act, they may be guilt y of different
offences by means of that ac t.
A attacks Z under such circumstances of grave provocation that his killi ng of Z would be only culpable homicide not
amounting to murder. B, having ill-will towards Z and intending to kill him, and not having been subject to the provocation,
assists A in killing Z. Here, though A and B are both engaged in causing Z's death, B is guilty of murder, and A is guilty only of
culpable homicide.

39. “Voluntarily ”.—A person is said to cause an effect “voluntarily ” when he causes it by means
whereby he intended to cause it, or by means which, at the time of employing those means, he knew or
had reason to believe to be likely to cause it.
A sets fire, by night, to an inhabited house in a large town, for the purpose of facilitating a robbery and thus causes the death
of a person. Here, A may not have intended to cause death, and may even be sorry that death has been caused by his act; yet, if he
knew that he was likely to cause death, he has caused death vo luntarily.

liable for his debts.

CHAPTER IV
GENERAL EXCEPTIONS
76. Act done by a person bound, or by mistake of fact believing himself bound, by law .—
Nothing is an offence which is done by a person who is, or who by reason of a mistak e of fact and not by
reason of a mistake of law in good faith believes himself to be, bound by law to do it.
(a) A, a soldier, fires on a mob by the order of his superior officer, in conformity with the commands of the law. A has
committed no offence.
(b) A, an officer of a Court of Justice, being ordered by that Court to arrest Y and, after due enquiry, believing Z to be Y,
arrests Z. A has committed no offence.
77. Act of Judge when acting judicially .—Nothing is an offence which is done by a Judge when
acting judicially in the exercise of any power which is, or which in good fait h he believes to be, given to
him by law.
78. Act done pursuant to the judgment or order of Court .—Nothing which is done in pursuance
of, or which is warranted by the judgment or order of, a Court of Justice, if done whilst such judgment or
order remains in force, is an offence, notwithstanding the Court may have had no jurisdicti on to pass such
judgment or order, provided the person doing the act in good faith believes that the Court had such
jurisdiction.
79. Act done by a person justified, or by mistake of fact believing himself justified, by la w.—
Nothing is an offence which is done by any person who is justified by law, or who by reason of a mistake
